I trained the solubility model and wrote predictions for all 100 test molecules to `predictions.csv`. It has the columns `smiles` and `logS`, the rows are in the same order as the input file, and no values are missing. Both commands are saved in `run.sh`.

**How the descriptors are scaled:** I used Chemprop's `v1_rdkit_2d_normalized` option. It calculates about 200 RDKit 2D descriptors for each molecule and rescales each one to between 0 and 1 using a fixed distribution fitted to known molecules. Many of these descriptors have a few very large values, which Chemprop's default scaling (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) handles poorly. Because the values are already scaled, I passed `--no-descriptor-scaling` to both training and prediction so they aren't scaled a second time.

**Training:**
- 30 epochs, stopping early if the validation score stopped improving for 10 epochs, with a fixed random seed so the run can be repeated.
- Chemprop's default random 80/10/10 split of the 400 training molecules into training, validation and test sets.
- Results on the held-out 10% (about 40 molecules): RMSE 0.61, MAE 0.49 and R² 0.88 (log units).

Because the split is random, the held-out molecules resemble the training ones, so these numbers may be optimistic for molecules that differ more from the training set.

The trained model is `runs/solubility/model_0/best.pt`, and the training log is `runs/solubility/train.log`.

I trained the model and saved predictions for all 100 test molecules to `predictions.csv`. It has the `smiles` and `logS` columns, in the same order as `data/solubility_test_inputs.csv`, with no missing values. On the 10% held-out split the test MSE was 0.375 (RMSE about 0.61 log units). That comes from roughly 40 molecules, so treat it as a rough estimate.

**On scaling the descriptors:** Chemprop's own docs say raw RDKit 2D descriptors fit its default StandardScaler poorly, because some of them have extremely skewed values (`Ipc`, for example). So I used the `v1_rdkit_2d_normalized` featurizer instead. It computes the RDKit 2D descriptors through descriptastorus and rescales each one to [0, 1] based on how its values are spread across a ChEMBL reference set. Because they're already scaled, I passed `--no-descriptor-scaling` so the CLI wouldn't apply a second scaling on top. The same featurizer is applied again when predicting.

**Commands (all in `run.sh`):**
- **`chemprop train`:** regression on `logS`, using the normalized RDKit 2D featurizer with no extra scaling. It splits the data 80/10/10, runs 30 epochs with fixed seeds, and writes the model to `solubility_model/`.
- **`chemprop predict`:** uses `solubility_model/model_0/best.pt` with the same featurizer to write `predictions.csv`.

The training log is in `train.log`. It reports no missing values in the train, validation or test splits.

The other approach in the docs is to compute the descriptors yourself, scale them, and pass them in with `--descriptors-path`. I didn't do that because the pre-normalized featurizer handles scaling entirely within the CLI. I trained a single model with no hyperparameter tuning.

I trained a 3-model Chemprop ensemble for `logS` with RDKit 2D descriptors as extra inputs, and wrote `predictions.csv`. It has the columns `smiles` and `logS` and 100 rows, in the same order as `data/solubility_test_inputs.csv`, with no missing values.

**How it's set up** (the commands are in `run.sh`):
- **Descriptors:** I used `--molecule-featurizers v1_rdkit_2d_normalized`. This computes the RDKit 2D descriptors and rescales each one to between 0 and 1 based on where it falls in the descriptor's overall distribution. That suits these descriptors better than Chemprop's default scaling, because many of them have extreme outliers. Since they're already scaled, I turned the default scaling off with `--no-descriptor-scaling`. The same featurizer is passed again in `chemprop predict`.
- **Training:** each model ran for 30 epochs, with early stopping after 10 epochs without improvement. Each of the 3 models used a different random 80/10/10 train/validation/test split, with a fixed seed so the run can be repeated. It ran on CPU.
- **Prediction:** `chemprop predict` averages the three models.

**Results on each model's held-out 10% test split:**

| Model | RMSE | MAE | R² |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.61 | 0.49 | 0.88 |
| 2 | 0.84 | 0.67 | 0.83 |
| 3 | 0.74 | 0.57 | 0.85 |

- **Few test molecules:** the training file has 400 molecules, so each test split holds only about 40 and these numbers are rough.
- **Easy splits:** random splits tend to make the model look better than it will on molecules unlike the training set.
- **Possibly undertrained:** the best checkpoints came at epochs 27–28 of the 30 allowed, so the models were probably still improving. More epochs would likely help, but I kept to your 30-epoch limit.

The models, splits and training log (`train.log`) are in `runs/solubility_rdkit2d/`.

I wrote `train.py`, ran it, and it produced `model.pt` and `predictions.csv`. On a held-out 10% of the training set, the model's predicted charges are off by 0.0065 per atom on average. A naive guess that splits each molecule's total charge evenly across its atoms is off by 0.103.

**How it works**
- **Model:** it uses Chemprop's `MolAtomBondMPNN` model type with only an atom-level output, trained for 30 epochs on 360 molecules, with the other 40 held out for checking.
- **Atom order:** atoms are read in exactly the order they appear in the SMILES. The script checks that each molecule's atom count matches the length of its training charge list.
- **Total charge per molecule:** the `data/` folder has `*_constraints.csv` files giving each molecule's total charge (`charge_sum`). I used these, which you didn't ask for: the model adjusts its predicted charges so they add up to that total, for both training and test molecules. Your training charges match these totals exactly, so I treated the test totals as known values. If the test totals aren't meant to be available when predicting, this setup doesn't fit and I'd need to change it.

**Checks on the output**
- `predictions.csv` has 100 rows in the same order as the test inputs, with columns `smiles` and `charges` in the same list format as the training data.
- Each list has one value per atom.
- Each molecule's charges add up to its given total, within 0.0005 because values are rounded to 4 decimals.
- `model.pt` loads back with `chemprop.models.load_model('model.pt', mol_atom_bond=True)`.

There's no GPU here, so training ran on the CPU. The final model was trained on 90% of the data, and I didn't retrain it on all 400 molecules.

I trained a per-atom charge model with the Chemprop Python API in `train.py`, ran it, and saved `model.pt` and `predictions.csv`. On a held-out 10% of the training molecules, the per-atom error averages 0.0033 (RMSE 0.0054), against 0.101 for just predicting the average charge every time.

**One thing to know first:** the model uses `data/partial_charges_test_constraints.csv`. That file gives each test molecule's total charge, and the model is built so its predicted charges for a molecule add up to exactly that total. They do, to within about 1e-6. In the training data these totals match the sums of the real charges exactly, so it's real information about each molecule. If you meant the test to be scored without it, the model would need to be retrained without that constraint, and the error would likely be higher.

**What I checked:**
- Charges in the training data cover heavy atoms only, in SMILES order (no hydrogens), and the count matches for every molecule.
- `predictions.csv` has the columns `smiles` and `charges` and 100 rows in the same order as the input file, each with one value per heavy atom, in the same list format as the training data.
- `model.pt` was saved with `chemprop.models.save_model` and loads back with `MolAtomBondMPNN.load_from_file`. The test predictions come from that reloaded model.

**How it was trained:**
- I used 360 molecules for training and held out 40 at random to pick the best epoch.
- It ran for 30 epochs on CPU with a fixed seed, batch size 16 and message-passing depth 4.
- The best score came at the last epoch, so more epochs would probably help a little; I stopped at 30 as you asked.
- Charges were rescaled for training and converted back for the output.

The 0.0033 error comes from just 40 molecules picked at random. Test molecules that look very different from the training set will probably have larger errors.

I wrote and ran `train.py`, which uses the Chemprop Python API to train an atom-level model for 30 epochs. On 40 molecules held out from training, predictions are off by 0.0079 on average per atom (RMSE 0.0147). Simply predicting the average charge for every atom would be off by 0.101.

**Charge sums:** I used the two charge-sum files in `data/` (`partial_charges_train_constraints.csv` and `partial_charges_test_constraints.csv`), which you didn't mention. In the training set, each value exactly equals the sum of that molecule's charges. The model is set up so each molecule's predicted charges add up to its value in these files; the largest mismatch was about 1e-6. So the test predictions rely on `partial_charges_test_constraints.csv`, and the model needs a charge sum for any new molecule you want to predict.

**Other details:**
- **Atoms:** the charges cover only the atoms written in the SMILES, not hydrogens. I checked that the counts match for all 400 training molecules.
- **Split:** I used a random 80/10/10 split, with 10% for picking the best epoch and 10% for the test score above. A random split usually overstates how well the model will do on molecules unlike the training set.
- **Training data:** the saved model was trained on 80% of the 400 molecules, not all of them. Retraining on everything would probably help a little, but then there's no data left to check it on.

I didn't try other model settings.

**Files:**
- `train.py`
- `model.pt`: reloads with `models.MolAtomBondMPNN.load_from_file`.
- `predictions.csv`: 100 rows with `smiles` and `charges`, in the input order and the training data's list format. Each list has one value per atom.

I saved predictions for all 100 test molecules to `predictions.csv`, with columns `smiles` and `logS` in the same order as the input file. The model is a blend: 80% a descriptor-based ensemble and 20% Chemprop. On 5-fold cross-validation over the training set, the blend's error (RMSE) is about **0.65 logS units**.

**What I compared (same 5-fold split for every model):**

| Model | Cross-validation RMSE |
|---|---|
| Chemprop with RDKit 2D descriptors added (3 models averaged per fold, 60 epochs) | 0.79 |
| Random forest on RDKit descriptors + Morgan fingerprints | 0.72 |
| Extra-trees, same features | 0.67 |
| Histogram gradient boosting, same features | 0.69 |
| Average of the three tree models | 0.66 |
| **0.2 × Chemprop + 0.8 × tree average** | **0.653** |

With only 400 training molecules, Chemprop on its own did worse than the descriptor-based models, but it still adds a little when blended in. For the final predictions, Chemprop was retrained on all the training data (5 models averaged) and the tree models were refit on all the data too.

**Caveats:**
- I chose the 0.2/0.8 blend weight using the same cross-validation predictions it's scored on, so 0.653 is slightly optimistic.
- Some training labels look noisy. For example, a chlorinated organophosphate is labelled logS 0.52, while every model predicts about −4.9. A few points like that probably account for much of the error.
- Everything ran on CPU (no GPU was available), so I kept Chemprop's training short to fit the 20 minutes. I didn't tune its hyperparameters.

Scripts are in `scripts/` (`desc.py`, `cp_cv.sh`, `blend.py`), and models and intermediate outputs are in `runs/`.

I've saved the predictions to `predictions.csv`: 100 rows with columns `smiles` and `logS`, in the same order as `data/solubility_test_inputs.csv`. I confirmed the row count and SMILES order match the input file.

**Model:** I fine-tuned the CheMeleon pretrained model, using the weights already saved on this machine, on the 400 training molecules. I trained it three times, each on a different random 80/10/10 split, and the predictions are the average of those three models. Training ran on CPU because no GPU was available.

**Comparison:** I also trained a standard Chemprop model with RDKit 2D descriptors on the same three splits. Error is RMSE in logS units on each split's 10% held-out portion:

| Model | Test RMSE per split | Mean RMSE | Mean R² |
|---|---|---|---|
| CheMeleon fine-tuned (used) | 0.45 / 0.67 / 0.64 | **0.59** | 0.91 |
| Chemprop + RDKit descriptors | 0.47 / 0.86 / 0.72 | 0.68 | 0.87 |

**Limitations:**
- Each held-out set has only about 40 molecules, so the RMSE varies a lot from split to split.
- The splits were random, so molecules unlike anything in the training set may have larger errors than these numbers suggest.
- Each model saw only 80% of the training data. I did not retrain on the full set or tune hyperparameters because of the 20-minute limit.

Model files are in `runs/chem/` and training logs are in `runs/*.log`.

I've saved the predictions to `predictions.csv`: 100 rows with columns `smiles` and `logS`, in the same order as `data/solubility_test_inputs.csv`, with no missing values.

**Model choice.** I compared two approaches on the same three random 80/10/10 splits of the 400 training molecules:

| Approach | Test RMSE per split | Mean RMSE |
|---|---|---|
| Fine-tuning the pretrained CheMeleon model | 0.45 / 0.67 / 0.64 | **0.59** (R² about 0.89–0.94) |
| Standard Chemprop network plus RDKit descriptors | 0.47 / 0.86 / 0.72 | 0.68 |

CheMeleon did better, so I used it. Its pretrained weights were already on the machine, so no internet was needed.

**Final model.** I averaged six CheMeleon models, each trained with a different seed and a different 90/10 train/validation split. This puts more of the data into training. Because of that, the final ensemble has no held-out test score of its own. The 0.59 RMSE from the comparison is the best estimate, and averaging six models should do at least as well. The splits were random, so expect a higher error on test molecules that look very different from the training set.

Everything ran on CPU because there's no GPU here. The trained models are in `runs/final/` and the training logs are in `runs/`.
